claim: Hydrogen storage methods include mechanical approaches like high pressures and low temperatures, and chemical compounds that release H2 on demand.
quote: These include mechanical approaches such as using high pressures and low temperatures, or employing chemical compounds that release H 2 upon demand.

claim: Compressed hydrogen storage involves keeping hydrogen gas under pressure to increase storage density.
quote: Compressed hydrogen is a storage form whereby hydrogen gas is kept under pressures to increase the storage density.

claim: Liquid hydrogen storage involves liquefying hydrogen by reducing its temperature to −253 °C.
quote: Hydrogen is liquefied by reducing its temperature to −253 °C, similar to liquefied natural gas (LNG) which is stored at −162 °C.

claim: Chemical storage of hydrogen can achieve high storage densities, with examples like methanol and dimethyl ether.
quote: Chemical storage could offer high storage performance due to the high storage densities.

claim: Nanomaterials can enhance hydrogen storage by improving sorption kinetics and storage capacity.
quote: Enhancement of sorption kinetics and storage capacity can be improved through nanomaterial-based catalyst doping.

claim: Metal hydrides are classified into inter-metallic, complex, and lightweight hydrides for hydrogen storage.
quote: There are three main classes of metal hydrides: Inter-metallic Hydrides, Complex Hydrides, Lightweight Hydrides.

claim: Electrochemical hydrogen storage allows controlled release of hydrogen using electricity.
quote: A most promising chemical approach is electrochemical hydrogen storage, as the release of hydrogen can be controlled by the applied electricity.

claim: Hydrogen storage in vehicles requires storing hydrogen in an energy-dense form for sufficient driving range.
quote: If it is to be used as fuel stored on board a vehicle, pure hydrogen gas must be stored in an energy-dense form to provide sufficient driving range.

claim: The release temperature of hydrogen storage materials affects the cost of chemical storage strategies.
quote: The energy or temperature to induce release affects the cost of any chemical storage strategy.

claim: Hydrogenation of CO2 to methanol is evaluated for hydrogen storage, but faces barriers like CO2 purification and energy inputs.
quote: Hydrogenation of CO 2 to methanol has been evaluated for hydrogen storage. Barriers of CO 2 hydrogenation includes purification of captured CO 2 , H 2 source from splitting water and energy inputs for hydrogenation.

claim: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are used for hydrogen storage due to their porous nature.
quote: MOFs are of interest for the storage of gases such as hydrogen and carbon dioxide.

claim: MOFs consist of metal clusters coordinated to organic ligands forming porous structures.
quote: MOFs are a class of coordination polymers consisting of metal clusters...coordinated to organic ligands to form...porous structures.

claim: MOFs are a subclass of coordination networks and coordination polymers.
quote: MOFs are a subclass of coordination networks...belong to coordination polymers.

claim: Hydrogen is widely regarded as an ideal energy storage medium due to its conversion capabilities.
quote: Hydrogen is...widely regarded as an ideal energy storage medium, due to the ease with which electricity can convert water into hydrogen and oxygen through electrolysis.

claim: Hydrogen technologies are applicable for many uses, including ammonia production and oil refining.
quote: Hydrogen is a chemical widely used in various applications including ammonia production, oil refining and energy.

claim: Hydrogen technologies can be carbon neutral and play a role in preventing climate change.
quote: Some hydrogen technologies are carbon neutral and could have a role in preventing climate change.

claim: Hydrogen is not a primary energy source because it is not naturally occurring as a fuel.
quote: Hydrogen is not a primary energy source , because it is not naturally occurring as a fuel.

claim: Hydrogen can be converted back to electrical power using a fuel cell or hydrogen turbine.
quote: ...can be converted back to electrical power using a fuel cell or hydrogen turbine.

claim: The potential environmental impact of hydrogen depends on the methods used to generate it as a fuel.
quote: The potential environmental impact depends primarily on the methods used to generate hydrogen as a fuel.

claim: Liquid hydrogen is the liquid state of hydrogen, used as a concentrated form of hydrogen storage.
quote: Liquid hydrogen is typically used as a concentrated form of hydrogen storage.

claim: Hydrogen must be cooled below 33 K to exist as a liquid, and to 20.28 K at atmospheric pressure.
quote: To exist as a liquid, H2 must be cooled below its critical point of 33 K.

claim: Liquid hydrogen storage takes less space than gaseous hydrogen at normal temperature and pressure.
quote: Storing it as liquid takes less space than storing it as a gas at normal temperature and pressure.

claim: Liquid hydrogen has a low density compared to other common fuels.
quote: However, the liquid density is very low compared to other common fuels.

claim: Hydrogen has two spin isomers: orthohydrogen and parahydrogen.
quote: There are two spin isomers of hydrogen.

claim: At cryogenic temperatures, hydrogen converts exothermically to parahydrogen.
quote: At cryogenic temperature it converts exothermically to parahydrogen.

claim: Catalytic conversion to parahydrogen during liquefaction avoids excessive boil-off in storage.
quote: To avoid the exothermic heat release and resulting excessive boil-off in storage, catalytic conversion to parahydrogen during liquefaction is employed.

claim: Theoretical minimum energy to liquefy hydrogen is 3.3 kWh/kg, increasing to 3.9 kWh/kg with para conversion.
quote: Hydrogen requires a theoretical minimum of 3.3 kWh/kg (12 MJ/kg) to liquefy, and 3.9 kWh/kg (14 MJ/kg) including converting the hydrogen to the para isomer.

claim: Existing liquefaction facilities use 10–13 kWh/kg, but future facilities may reduce this to 6.5 kWh/kg.
quote: Existing liquefaction facilities use 10–13 kWh/kg...future facilities are expected to cut the specific energy demand by half to 6.5 kWh/kg.

claim: Hydrail vehicles use hydrogen fuel for propulsion, either by burning it in an engine or using a fuel cell.
quote: Hydrail vehicles use the chemical energy of hydrogen for propulsion, either by burning hydrogen in a hydrogen internal combustion engine, or by reacting hydrogen with oxygen in a fuel cell.

claim: Hydrail vehicles are hybrid vehicles with renewable energy storage like batteries or super capacitors.
quote: Hydrail vehicles are usually hybrid vehicles with renewable energy storage, such as batteries or super capacitors, for regenerative braking.

claim: Hydrail applications include various types of rail transport, such as commuter and freight rail.
quote: Potential hydrail applications include all types of rail transport: commuter rail; passenger rail; freight rail; light rail; rail rapid transit; mine railways; industrial railway systems; trams; and special rail rides at parks and museums.

claim: Hydrail technology is part of the proposed hydrogen economy for rail transportation.
quote: Widespread use of hydrogen for fueling rail transportation is a basic element of the proposed hydrogen economy.

claim: Hydrail technology is related to hydrogen storage but focuses on transportation applications.
quote: Many of the same technologies that can be applied to hydrail vehicles can be applied to other forms of transport as well, such as road vehicles.
